analysis.one_liner: Limits brand drug companies to one patent-based delay of a generic competitor's approval.
analysis.headline: The bill has gone no further than introduction: it was referred to the Senate health committee on July 31, 2025, and no hearing or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug company tries to bring a cheaper copy of a brand-name drug to market, the brand can sue over its patents — and each patent suit can freeze the FDA's approval of the generic for up to 30 months while the case is decided. Filing suits on patent after patent can stretch that freeze out for years. This bill would let a brand-name drug maker pick only one patent that can trigger that 30-month delay, and the choice would be locked in. That would make it harder to stall cheap generic drugs through repeated patent litigation.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need brand-name drugs would benefit if the bill passes: generics reaching the market sooner generally means lower prices at the pharmacy. Generic drug makers also gain, since their approvals would be frozen less often and less predictably by brand patent suits.

how_it_helps.text: It caps the automatic 30-month FDA approval delay for generics at litigation over a single patent chosen by the brand, instead of a stay for every patent asserted.
The chosen patent cannot be changed or amended later, closing a route brand firms could use to add new stays as a generic nears approval.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies would bear the cost, losing a legal tool that extends the period they can sell a drug without generic competition and keep prices high.

drawbacks.text: The 30-month stay exists to give patent holders a window to enforce legitimate patents; restricting it to one patent could let generic firms challenge weakly protected patents in parallel and reach market before a brand's secondary patents are fully litigated.
The bill only applies to drugs approved after enactment, so patients on existing brand drugs see no change until new approvals accumulate under the rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — earlier generic competition on drugs where brand firms stack patent suits — could be large for patients paying brand-name prices. The cost is a genuine trade-off: brand firms would keep full patent rights but lose the leverage of multiple sequential 30-month stays, which some argue protects legitimate patent enforcement. The design is narrow and targeted rather than sweeping, which limits both its benefit and its risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 31, 2025 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action has been taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no companion action in the House appears in the record.
It carries a single Republican cosponsor, Sen. Cassidy, alongside Democratic sponsor Sen. Durbin.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off so far: as long as the bill sits in committee, they keep the ability to delay generic competition with multiple patent suits. Patients paying brand prices gain nothing until it moves.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it to the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-LA), cosponsor and ranking member of the Senate health committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship in the committee that would consider it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — both also in the relevant committee — but no floor vote has occurred to test broader partisan support.

industries.note: They would lose the ability to trigger a 30-month FDA approval delay for each of a drug's many patents, which has been used to keep generics off the market for years at a time.
Faster, more predictable generic approvals would reduce the litigation risk of bringing low-cost copies to market.
Unaffected directly, but they benefit from cheaper generics through lower drug costs; no provision touches their role.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the HELP Committee with no scheduled hearing or markup. Bipartisan patent bills in this area have historically struggled against pharmaceutical industry resistance, and with only two sponsors so far, the most likely path is that it remains dormant in committee for the rest of the Congress unless the committee leadership chooses to take it up.
